profile.beat: A high-beta SMID-cap position trader who runs a thematic basket portfolio (AI infrastructure/neocloud, edge-inference hardware, enterprise software/cybersecurity, solar) and pairs it with a heavy market-wire feed of macro headlines - Fed/Warsh, treasury yields, oil and the Iran war, tariffs, and the Korean market. Roughly half the timeline is verbatim headline reposting and earnings prints; the stance-bearing content sits in his replies and occasional long-form essays.
profile.style: Theme first, then a subset with pricing power, then names validated on his self-described three pillars: fundamental valuation, technical health, thematic relevance. He talks constantly about position sizing, cost basis and 'incrementally moving the exposure meter' rather than binary calls, and he is explicit that he sells into weakness to protect the equity curve. Conviction language is direct and combative in replies ('I still believe is a value-trap', 'my horse has been $NBIS since last May'), and he freely admits mistakes in sizing, leverage and options. He argues valuation matters even inside momentum themes, but rejects the label of value investor.
profile.cadence: Very high volume and reply-dominated - 357 of 495 posts are replies. Recurring formats: all-caps newswire headlines with an asterisk prefix, earnings beat/miss scorecards, a weekly 'Portfolio update posted at...' post pointing to a paid Discord, long weekend essays on market structure or AI capex, and chart/level commentary on the indexes.
profile.revisits: Yes, persistently. He tracks the same names across weeks - NBIS from 2077193789907534038 to 2079599935893147953 to 2088310222817243397 to 2089497613762498989, the software basket from 2077178812945584456 to 2077821873975423246 to 2086896512160895347, AMKR through 2080404461961261127 and 2081835606171115732 - and he publicly revises his own framework, notably reversing his long-standing dismissal of AI bear arguments in 2077912967803256905 and following up his own thesis with a rebuttal thread in 2077986379292700750.
profile.caveats: Heavy conflict of interest: he runs a paid Discord and states outright that he does not share his portfolio, entries, exits or sizing on X (2077194343215984654) - the public feed is a marketing surface for a subscription. Performance claims are self-reported brokerage screenshots that cannot be verified from the text. Names frequently surface publicly only after they have already worked, framed as victory laps citing a much earlier private entry (TENB in 2075237173675077936, OSS in 2077255869079679102, NBIS in 2087568715067887736), which biases any measured public record upward at entry and downward at exit. He also repeatedly announces that he cut or exited positions without naming them (2080339947723059428, 2080393281662308427, 2087573933138563529), so the public timeline systematically misses his sells. Many posts are pure headline reposts with no stance at all, and several stance-bearing replies omit the ticker, so they are only interpretable from the thread context.

narrative: The window opens with him already in a painful drawdown from a historic momentum unwind: he describes the Goldman and Morgan Stanley momentum indexes posting their worst readings on record (2077528883184726028), and frames his own book as AI/hardware names unwinding while a newer enterprise-software basket acts as shelter (2077821873975423246). His central intellectual turn comes on July 16-20, when China's Moonshot 'Kimi K3' and Alibaba's 'Qwen 3.8 Max' land: after three years of, in his words, whistling past the bearish arguments, he starts questioning the pricing power of U.S. frontier labs and the durability of the capex that the whole AI trade discounts (2077878579166134622, 2077912967803256905). He explicitly refuses the AI-bear label and instead lands on a 'decentralization of compute' framework - compute demand is fine, but the capex burden fragments away from the hyperscalers, which he reads as structurally bullish for cloud compute broadly (2079146204714188912). Through late July he acts on the drawdown rather than debating it, cutting peripheral, weak-cost-basis positions while holding core names, and blaming his own leverage and single-stock risk rules rather than the market (2080339947723059428, 2080762894556217708). From the end of July the driver of his commentary switches from AI narrative to macro: he decides yields and oil, not the capex debate, are what is actually pressuring stocks (2080469549783056650), and repeats that treasury yields must fall before risk appetite returns (2083202728474337499). August is spent almost entirely on the bond vigilantes, Warsh and the Iran war, which he argues is the single accessible kill-switch for rates (2093414141801202008). His book-level positioning by late August is still very net long but with cash raised and ready to redeploy if yields cooperate (2092742658368151867). Individual-name conviction ends the window higher rather than lower: NBIS squeezes and he takes a victory lap on it, he publishes a detailed fundamental case for MITK, and after OKTA/CRWD/CRM prints he calls software and cybersecurity back into leadership.

picks.prospect: Continued upside in the one neocloud he is willing to own, on the strength of its team, execution and contracted backlog as compute demand keeps broadening.
picks.risk_reward: He addressed the risk directly and unusually well: neoclouds are the hardest part of the AI buildout to value because GPU depreciation and long-term rental pricing are still unknowable, and anything capex-reliant worries him. He offsets that by holding it as a deliberately small, speculative sleeve and by a deep cost-basis advantage that lets him sit through drawdowns.
picks.thesis: Of all the neoclouds he screens, only one clears his bar on team, talent, execution and quality of contracted backlog, so he concentrates his entire neocloud exposure in it rather than spreading across the group. He treats it as an investment position rather than a trade and has held it since well before the window.
